opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few dynamics that push in that direction, and they compound over time.

The most basic one is that as AI systems get more capable, the value of human labor starts to fall relative to the value of compute and the models themselves. Historically, broad-based prosperity has been tied to the fact that you need lots of people to do lots of work. If you can increasingly substitute AI for human labor, especially cognitive labor at first and then physical labor via robotics, that link weakens. The returns flow more to whoever owns the compute, the models, and the key infrastructure, rather than being spread across workers.

Second, I expect the frontier to be quite concentrated. Training the best systems requires enormous capital, specialized talent, and access to chips, and there are strong economies of scale. So you plausibly end up with a small number of companies, and maybe a couple of governments, controlling the most capable systems. And if the best AIs are themselves accelerating AI research, the leading developers can pull further ahead. Being slightly ahead could translate into being much more ahead, rather than everyone converging.

Third, there's an access gradient even within those organizations. Early on, the most capable systems may be used internally first, for AI R&D, for strategic advantage, maybe without being released at all, or released in weaker forms. So the people who benefit most are those closest to the frontier: the companies, their employees and investors, and whoever has influence over them. That's a much smaller group than "society broadly."

And finally, many of the mechanisms that usually redistribute gains, like competitive labor markets, democratic pressure, and the state needing a productive, cooperative population for tax revenue and military power, could weaken if AI can do most of the work. If those that control the AI no longer depend on the broad population in the same way, the bargaining power of ordinary people falls.

None of this is inevitable. Policy, deliberate commitments to broad distribution, or just a more diffuse technology landscape could push the other way. But absent deliberate effort, my default expectation is that the gains concentrate more and more among people with proximity to and control over the most capable AI systems, and that concentration of wealth can also become a concentration of power, which I think is one of the more worrying aspects.

r001.rationale: The response says employees of frontier companies may benefit, but does not predict that AI company employees will become more highly paid when AI automates those companies.

r002.rationale: It discusses compute ownership and the capital needed to train frontier systems, but does not argue that rising AI intellectual labor value will sharply increase compute prices in short-timeline scenarios with scarce compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic picture is that when you're an AI developer, you have a bunch of advantages that nobody else has. You have the frontier models before anyone else does, you have way more compute, you can run them at much higher volumes without worrying about rate limits or cost, and you can fine-tune them for exactly the thing you care about. And the thing AI developers care about most is AI research, because that's where the returns compound.

So you get this loop where the people closest to the models are the ones best positioned to apply them, and the thing they're applying them to is making the models better, which widens the gap further. I think of it as: if you're an engineer at an AI company, you're using the model that's maybe six months ahead of what's publicly available, and you have internal tooling built specifically to let it do your job. Someone running a logistics company or a law firm is using the public version, through a chat interface or a product that some startup built, and the integration work hasn't been done yet.

And integration is actually a big part of this. Automating a job isn't just "the model is smart enough." You need the scaffolding, the access to systems, the ability to iterate on the failure cases. AI companies have very strong incentives to do that work for their own research. They have much weaker incentives, at least for a while, to do it for everyone else, because the returns elsewhere are more diffuse and slower.

So my expectation is that for some period, maybe a couple of years, you see AI research and adjacent engineering being substantially automated while most of the economy looks surprisingly normal. The benefits accrue to a pretty small group of people and organizations, and the broader diffusion lags. Eventually that gap closes, because the capabilities become good enough and cheap enough that the integration work is easy, or the AIs do the integration work themselves. But the transition period is where a lot of the weirdness happens, and I think people underrate how uneven it's going to look from the outside.

r001.rationale: The response says AI company employees are well positioned to benefit from automation, but it does not predict that their pay will rise when AI can automate AI companies.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI developers having more compute, but does not argue that scarce compute prices will rise sharply as AI intellectual labour becomes more valuable.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot depends on which things remain scarce as AI gets more capable. If you can automate most of the labor involved in producing something, then owning the systems that do that work, or owning the compute they run on, becomes relatively more important. And earning money by selling your labor becomes relatively less important. So there’s a fairly straightforward reason to expect the owners of AI companies and compute to capture a larger fraction of income.

There’s also an information and control advantage. People close to AI are more likely to understand what the systems can do, see changes coming, and be in a position to act on them. If progress is very fast, other people might not have much time to catch up before consequential decisions have already been made.

But I’d distinguish that from saying ordinary people won’t benefit. You could have much cheaper goods and services, and that could be a huge improvement for almost everyone, while wealth and decision-making power become much more concentrated. And the extent of that concentration depends on things like how competitive the AI market is and whether governments redistribute the gains. I don’t think it’s inevitable, but I think there are strong pressures in that direction.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that owners of AI companies and compute may capture more income, but does not say AI company employees will become more highly paid when AI automates those companies.

r002.rationale: The response says compute ownership may become more important, but does not claim that rising AI intellectual labor value will sharply increase compute prices in short-timeline scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that as AI can do more of the work, there’s less need to bring in people who aren’t already involved. If you’re running an AI company, you might initially need lots of employees and outside expertise. But if AI can provide those things, a smaller group can accomplish much more without sharing ownership or control with additional people.

And the people closest to AI are likely to be best positioned to recognize what it can do, deploy it effectively, and use it to improve the next generation of systems. So you can get a feedback loop where an initial advantage translates into more resources and more control over further automation.

That doesn’t mean other people get no benefits. They could get cheaper goods and much better services. But there’s a distinction between benefiting as a consumer and having a substantial share of the income or influence. I’m more concerned that the latter becomes concentrated, especially if human labor stops being an important source of bargaining power.

r001.rationale: The response says a smaller group may gain more control and resources, but it does not predict that AI company employees will become more highly paid as AI automates AI companies.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss short timelines, scarce compute, rising AI intellectual labor value, or compute prices rising sharply.
